name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
summary: Privacy is a fundamental right. The Constitution does not name it, but it is part of the right to life and personal liberty in Article 21, and of the other freedoms in Part III.
question: Is privacy a fundamental right under the Constitution of India?
If it is, were M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh wrong to say that the Constitution does not protect it?
principles: Rights can sit inside other rights. A freedom the text never names can still be fundamental, if it forms part of one that is named.
Dignity and the freedom to run one's own life lie at the core of Part III.
Privacy belongs to the person, not to a place. A person does not lose it by stepping into a public space.
So life and liberty are not gifts from the Constitution. Every person has them already, and the Constitution recognises them.

name: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla
summary: During the 1975 Emergency, the Court held by 4 votes to 1 that a detained person could not go to court to challenge the detention, even if it was illegal or made in bad faith. Justice H.R. Khanna dissented.
question: The President had suspended the right to go to any court to enforce Articles 14, 21 and 22. While that order lasted, could a detained person still ask a High Court for habeas corpus?
Could the person at least argue that the detention order was illegal, or was made in bad faith?
principles: Justice Khanna's view is now the law. The State needs the authority of a law to hold anyone, whether or not Article 21 can be enforced at the time.
A dissent can become the law later. Khanna's did, forty-one years on.
So the case is remembered as a warning. Courts matter most to personal liberty when the State is at its most powerful.

name: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
summary: A divorced Muslim woman who cannot support herself can claim a monthly allowance from her former husband under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, like any other woman.
question: Can a divorced Muslim woman claim maintenance from her former husband under Section 125 CrPC?
Muslim personal law makes the husband pay only for the iddat period. Does that end his duty under Section 125?
Is mahr a "sum payable on divorce", so that paying it frees the husband from maintenance under Section 127(3)(b)?
principles: Laws that prevent destitution are secular. They apply to everyone, and personal law cannot take them away.
The Court's remark that Article 44 "has remained a dead letter" was said in passing. The remark did not decide the case, but it started a long debate on a common civil code.
So religion decides much of family law, but not whether a woman is left without support.

name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India
aka: The NJAC case, or the Fourth Judges case
summary: The Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act, which had given the government a say in choosing judges. The independence of the judiciary is part of the basic structure, so the collegium of senior judges came back.
question: Were the 99th Amendment (2014) and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act (2014) valid?
The new commission included the Law Minister and two eminent persons from outside the judiciary. Did that break the independence of the judiciary, which is part of the basic structure?
principles: How judges are chosen is part of judicial independence. So rules on appointments are tested against the basic structure, like any other amendment.
So the judges kept control of appointments, but the Court accepted that the collegium had to become more open.

name: Kehar Singh v. Union of India
summary: When deciding a mercy petition under Article 72, the President can look at the evidence afresh and take a different view from the courts. The President acts on the advice of the ministers, and the petitioner has no right to an oral hearing.
question: When considering a mercy petition under Article 72, can the President look at the evidence and differ from the Supreme Court on guilt or sentence?
Does the petitioner have a right to be heard in person by the President?
Can the courts review how the pardon power is used, and are guidelines needed?
principles: So a mercy petition is a real second look at the case, not a formality. But it is a political decision, not a fresh trial.

name: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
summary: A long, unexplained delay in deciding a mercy petition is a ground to change a death sentence to life imprisonment, in every kind of case. The death sentences of 15 convicts were changed, and the Court laid down safeguards for prisoners on death row.
question: After a death sentence becomes final, can delay in deciding the mercy petition be a ground to reduce the sentence?
Does this ground apply to offences under anti-terror laws such as TADA?
Are mental illness and solitary confinement grounds for relief?
What safeguards should protect prisoners on death row?
principles: So waiting for years under a death sentence is itself a punishment. When the State causes that wait, the State loses the right to carry out the execution.

name: Samsher Singh v. State of Punjab
summary: The President and the Governor are constitutional heads. They act on the advice of their Council of Ministers, except where the Constitution gives the Governor a discretion. The orders ending the service of two judicial officers on probation were set aside.
question: Must the Governor be personally satisfied before removing an officer on probation, or can the Governor act on the advice of ministers?
Were the orders ending the service of two judicial officers on probation really punishments, which needed an inquiry under Article 311?
Did the High Court properly use its control over the lower judiciary under Article 235?
principles: So power rests with the elected ministers, not with the formal head of State. The head of State advises and warns, but follows the ministers' advice.

name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
result: Majority on the main points, in six opinions
summary: A proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 can be reviewed by the courts. A government's majority must be tested by a vote in the House, and the Assembly cannot be dissolved before Parliament approves the proclamation. Secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution.
question: Can the courts review a proclamation under Article 356, and how far?
Does Article 74(2) stop the courts from seeing the material behind a proclamation?
Can the Assembly be dissolved before Parliament approves the proclamation, and can a dismissed government be restored?
Could the governments of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh be dismissed after the demolition of the Babri Masjid?
principles: Federalism is part of the basic structure. The States are not mere agents of the Centre.
So the Centre can no longer dismiss a State government on a Governor's say-so. The Centre must show relevant reasons, and the majority is counted in the House.

name: Shivraj Singh Chouhan v. Speaker, Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly
aka: The Madhya Pradesh floor test case
summary: A Governor can ask a government to prove its majority in the House, even while the House is sitting, if there is objective material to doubt its majority. But the power must not be used to topple an elected government.
question: Can the Governor call for a floor test while the Assembly is in session?
On what material may the Governor act?
Does the Governor's direction interfere with the Speaker's power over resignations?
principles: So when a majority is in doubt, the House decides it quickly by a vote. Neither the Governor nor a delay by the Speaker can decide it for the members.

name: Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of Andhra Pradesh
summary: Orders of pardon or remission under Articles 72 and 161 can be reviewed by the courts on limited grounds. A Governor's order cutting a sentence, based on irrelevant and political considerations, was set aside.
question: Can a court review an order of remission passed by the Governor under Article 161?
On what grounds can such an order be set aside?
principles: Courts check how a mercy decision was made, not whether mercy was deserved.
So mercy cannot be handed out as a political favour. A pardon based on party loyalty can be struck down.

name: P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (CBI/SPE)
summary: By 3 votes to 2, members of Parliament who took bribes and then voted as agreed were held immune from prosecution under Article 105(2). A member who took a bribe but did not vote, and those who paid, were not immune. The ruling was overruled in Sita Soren (2024).
question: Does Article 105(2) protect a member of Parliament from prosecution for taking a bribe to vote in a particular way?
Does Article 105(3) give any such immunity?
Is a member of Parliament a public servant under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988?
principles: So the result was strange. The member who took the money and voted as paid was safe, while the member who took the money and stayed away was not.

name: Sita Soren v. Union of India
summary: Members of Parliament and State legislatures have no immunity from prosecution for taking bribes, even when the bribe is for a vote or a speech in the House. P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998) was overruled.
question: Do Articles 105(2) and 194(2) protect a legislator from prosecution for taking a bribe to vote or speak in a particular way?
Was P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998) rightly decided?
principles: Parliamentary privilege protects the free working of the House, not the private gain of its members.
So the protection for a legislator's vote does not protect a vote that was sold.

name: Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha
summary: Each House of Parliament can expel a member, as part of its privileges under Article 105(3). The courts can review that power for illegality or unconstitutionality, but not for mere mistakes of procedure.
question: Do the Houses of Parliament have the power to expel a member?
Given the bar in Article 122, can the courts review how a House uses its privileges, and how far?
principles: So the House can throw out members who sold their questions. But the courts keep a narrow power to check that the House acted within the Constitution.

name: Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd.
aka: The tribunals and Money Bill case
summary: The rules made under the Finance Act, 2017 for appointing tribunal members were struck down for weakening judicial independence. Whether that part of the Act could be passed as a Money Bill was sent to a larger bench.
question: Part XIV of the Finance Act, 2017 changed the working of many tribunals. Was it validly passed as a Money Bill?
Did Section 184 of the Act give the government too much power to make rules?
Were the Tribunal Rules, 2017, made under Section 184, valid?
principles: Tribunals that take over the work of courts must be independent of the government, especially in appointments and tenure.
So the government cannot pick and control the people who decide cases against it.

name: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Aadhaar)
summary: The Aadhaar Act, 2016 was upheld, and its passage as a Money Bill was accepted. But private companies cannot demand Aadhaar, and it cannot be made compulsory for bank accounts, mobile connections or school admissions.
question: Does the Aadhaar scheme break the right to privacy?
Was the Aadhaar Act validly passed as a Money Bill?
Which uses of Aadhaar are valid?
principles: So Aadhaar survived as a tool for delivering welfare, but not as a key that every bank, phone company and school could demand.

name: D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar
summary: The Governor of Bihar kept making the same ordinances again and again without placing them before the legislature. The Court called this a fraud on the Constitution. The government cannot take over the law-making power of the legislature.
question: Can the Governor keep an ordinance alive for ever by re-making it after each session of the legislature?
Does a member of the public have the standing to challenge such a practice?
principles: What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. The rule binds every constitutional power, not only the power to make ordinances.
So an ordinance may bridge a gap while the legislature is away, but may not become a way of governing.

name: Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar
summary: Re-making ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution. Every ordinance must be laid before the legislature, and the courts can review the satisfaction behind it.
question: Is it valid to re-make an ordinance again and again without placing it before the legislature?
Is the duty to lay an ordinance before the legislature mandatory?
Can the courts review the satisfaction on which an ordinance is made?
Do rights created by an ordinance survive after it lapses?
principles: So an ordinance is a bridge to a law, not a replacement for one. The legislature must get its chance to vote on it.

name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India
summary: In appointing and transferring judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts, the opinion of the Chief Justice of India, formed with senior judges, must prevail. S.P. Gupta (1981) was overruled on this point, and the collegium system began.
question: In appointments to the Supreme Court and the High Courts, and in transfers of High Court judges, must the opinion of the Chief Justice of India prevail?
Can the courts decide how many judges a High Court should have?
principles: So the power to choose judges moved from the government to the judges themselves. The group of senior judges who choose came to be called the collegium.

name: In re Special Reference No. 1 of 1998
summary: Answering a question from the President, the Court held that the Chief Justice of India must consult a collegium of senior judges. For the Supreme Court, the collegium is the Chief Justice and the four senior most judges. A recommendation made without that consultation does not bind the government.
question: What does "consultation with the Chief Justice of India" require in appointments and transfers of judges?
Who must be consulted, and how?
Is a recommendation that does not follow these rules binding on the government?
principles: So the collegium took its present shape: five senior judges for the Supreme Court, recording their views in writing.

name: State of Karnataka v. Union of India
summary: A State can sue the Union under Article 131 when Central action touches the State's powers of government. But the Centre could appoint a Commission of Inquiry into charges against Karnataka's Chief Minister and ministers, so Karnataka's suit was dismissed.
question: Can a State bring a suit under Article 131 against the Centre's appointment of a Commission of Inquiry into its ministers?
Could the Central Government appoint such a commission under Section 3 of the Commissions of Inquiry Act?
principles: So Karnataka won the right to come to the Court, but lost the case. The federal structure did not protect State ministers from a Central inquiry.

name: Pritam Singh v. The State
summary: The Supreme Court's power to grant special leave to appeal under Article 136 is to be used rarely, only in exceptional cases where grave injustice has been done. The Court is not an ordinary court of criminal appeal.
question: When should the Supreme Court grant special leave to appeal under Article 136?
Will the Court look again at the facts found in a criminal case?
principles: Article 136 gives a remedy at the Court's choice, not a right of appeal.
So the Supreme Court keeps itself for grave injustice and important questions, not for a third trial of the facts.

name: Bengal Immunity Co. Ltd. v. State of Bihar
summary: The Supreme Court is not bound by its own earlier decisions and can overrule them when convinced they are wrong. The Court overruled State of Bombay v. United Motors (1953) and held that States could not tax sales between States until Parliament allowed it.
question: Is the Supreme Court bound by its own earlier decisions?
Under Article 286 as it then stood, could a State tax sales made in the course of trade between States before Parliament made a law?
principles: A mistaken reading of the Constitution deserves correction more readily than one of a statute, because the Constitution is so much harder to amend.
So the Court's own past rulings bind every other court, but not the Court itself, which can correct its own mistakes.

name: Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India
summary: The Bhopal gas disaster settlement of US $470 million was upheld on review. But the Court set aside the quashing of the criminal cases and revived the prosecutions. The Court also held that no ordinary law can limit its power under Article 142.
question: Could the Supreme Court, under Article 142, take over the civil suits and criminal cases and end them by recording a settlement?
Was the quashing of the criminal cases as part of the settlement valid?
Was the settlement void because the victims were not heard, or because it went against public policy?
principles: So the company's money settled the claims for compensation, but it could not buy the accused freedom from trial.

name: Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India
summary: The Supreme Court cannot suspend a lawyer's licence to practise as a punishment for contempt. The power to suspend belongs to the Bar Councils under the Advocates Act, and Article 142 cannot be used to take it over. In re Vinay Chandra Mishra (1995) was overruled on this point.
question: When punishing a lawyer for contempt, can the Supreme Court suspend the lawyer's licence to practise?
Can Article 142 be used to exercise a power that a law gives to another body?
principles: So even the Court's widest power works inside the law, not above it.

name: Dr. M. Ismail Faruqui v. Union of India
result: Act upheld by 3:2, except one section; Reference returned
summary: The law by which the Centre took over the land at Ayodhya was upheld, except the section that ended all pending court cases over the disputed site. The Court declined to answer the President's question on whether a Hindu temple had stood there.
question: Was the Acquisition of Certain Area at Ayodhya Act, 1993 valid?
Could the Act end all pending suits about the disputed site without providing another way to settle the dispute?
Should the Court answer the President's question under Article 143?
principles: So the dispute went back to the ordinary courts. The Court refused to settle a question of history and faith by giving an opinion.

name: Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers v. Union of India
aka: The CAG audit of telecom companies case
summary: The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) can examine the accounts of private telecom companies that share their revenue with the government, to check that the Union gets its due share. Spectrum is a natural resource that the State holds in trust for the people.
question: Can the CAG audit the accounts of private telecom companies?
Does the sharing of revenue under their licences bring their accounts within the CAG's powers under Article 149?
principles: So a private company that profits from public spectrum cannot hide from the public auditor the figures on which the public's share depends.

name: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker, Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly
result: Unanimous in result, in three opinions
summary: The Governor of Arunachal Pradesh acted unconstitutionally when, without the ministers' advice, he brought the Assembly session forward and directed its business. The Court set aside everything done under those orders and restored the position of 15 December 2015.
question: Can the Governor summon the Assembly, bring its session forward or direct its business in the Governor's own discretion?
Can the courts review the Governor's use of discretion under Article 163?
principles: So a Governor cannot take sides in a party's internal revolt by changing the Assembly's calendar. The elected government decides when the House meets.

name: State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab
summary: A Governor who withholds assent to a Bill must send it back to the legislature to be reconsidered. The Governor cannot simply sit on Bills and so veto the work of an elected legislature.
question: Can a Governor withhold assent to a Bill without sending it back to the legislature?
The Speaker called the Assembly back for a session that had been adjourned but not prorogued. Was that sitting valid?
principles: So the Governor may ask the legislature to think again, but the legislature has the last word on its own Bills.

name: State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu
summary: The Governor of Tamil Nadu acted illegally when he withheld assent to ten Bills and then, after they were passed again, reserved them for the President. The Court set time limits for Governors and the President and treated the Bills as approved. A later advisory opinion rejected the time limits and the deemed approval.
question: What choices does a Governor have under Article 200, and must the Governor act on the ministers' advice?
Can a Governor reserve for the President a Bill that the legislature has passed again?
Can the courts set time limits, and treat Bills as approved?
principles: So the judgment's core point against endless delay survived. But five judges rejected its time limits and its deemed approval seven months later.

name: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India
summary: The power of the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227, and of the Supreme Court under Article 32, to review laws and decisions is part of the basic structure. Tribunals can hear cases first, but a bench of two High Court judges can review their decisions.
question: Can Articles 323A and 323B shut out the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227, and the Supreme Court under Article 32?
Can tribunals decide whether laws and rules are constitutional?
Do tribunals replace the High Courts, or only add to them?
principles: So a tribunal can take the first look at a dispute, but its decision always remains open to a High Court.

name: Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks, Mumbai
summary: Having another remedy does not stop a High Court from hearing a writ petition. The High Court can still hear one where a fundamental right is at stake, natural justice is broken, the action is wholly without legal power, or a law is challenged as invalid.
question: Can a High Court dismiss a writ petition only because the petitioner has another remedy under a law?
Did the Registrar of Trade Marks have the power to issue a notice to cancel Whirlpool's renewal while cases about the mark were pending in the High Court?
principles: So the High Court's door stays open where the problem is serious. The other remedy is a rule of convenience, not a lock.

name: Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India
summary: The Lieutenant Governor of Delhi must act on the advice of the elected Council of Ministers, except on public order, police and land. The Lieutenant Governor has no independent power to decide, and should refer differences to the President only in exceptional cases.
question: Who holds executive power in Delhi: the Lieutenant Governor or the elected government?
Must the Lieutenant Governor act on the advice of the Council of Ministers?
When can the Lieutenant Governor refer a difference of opinion to the President?
principles: So the people's vote in Delhi decides who governs most matters. The Lieutenant Governor is not a parallel ruler.

name: Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India
summary: The elected Government of Delhi controls the civil servants who work for it, except those dealing with public order, police and land. The Lieutenant Governor must act on its advice on services. But Parliament reversed the effect of the judgment within months.
question: Does the Government of NCT of Delhi control the civil servants working in Delhi?
Does Entry 41 of the State List, on services, fall within the powers of the Delhi Assembly?
principles: An elected government must control the officers who carry out its decisions.
So the Court can read the Constitution in favour of an elected government. But Parliament can still change the law on which that reading rests.

name: Kishan Singh Tomar v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Ahmedabad
summary: Elections to a municipality must be completed before its five-year term ends. Redrawing ward boundaries and other administrative reasons cannot justify delay, and the State Election Commission has wide powers to make sure elections are held on time.
question: Is the rule in Article 243U(3), that municipal elections must be completed before the term ends, mandatory?
Can a State Election Commission delay elections in order to redraw ward boundaries?
principles: Local bodies must not be left without elected members because of administrative delay.
So a city cannot be run by officials alone because the government is slow to redraw its wards. The vote comes first.

name: Vikas Kishanrao Gawali v. State of Maharashtra
aka: The local bodies OBC reservation case
summary: Reservation for Other Backward Classes in local bodies is valid only if the State meets a "triple test". The State needs a dedicated commission, a share fixed for each local body on its findings, and total reservation of no more than 50 per cent.
question: Maharashtra reserved 27 per cent of seats in its zilla parishads and panchayat samitis for backward classes. Is that valid where it takes total reservation above 50 per cent?
What must a State do before reserving seats for Other Backward Classes in local bodies?
principles: So a State cannot carry over a flat 27 per cent quota into local bodies. The State must study each place first and stay within half the seats.

name: Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce Ltd., Khulna
result: Act upheld by the Privy Council
summary: A law is judged by its "pith and substance", meaning its true nature. If in substance it falls within the legislature's own list, it is valid even though it touches a subject in another list along the way. The Bengal Money-lenders Act, 1940 was upheld.
question: Did the Bengal Money-lenders Act, 1940 fall within the provincial subject of money-lending, or did it invade the federal subject of promissory notes?
Is a law invalid because it touches, along the way, a subject outside the legislature's power?
principles: So a money-lending law stays a money-lending law, even if it affects the promissory notes on which loans are given.

name: State of West Bengal v. Kesoram Industries Ltd.
aka: The coal and tea cess case
summary: West Bengal's cesses on coal-bearing land and on tea estates were upheld. The power to tax is a separate subject in the lists, the way a tax is measured does not decide what it is, and royalty is not a tax.
question: Were West Bengal's cesses on coal-bearing land, tea estates and minor minerals valid State taxes?
Did Parliament's laws on mines and minerals and on tea take away the State's power to levy them?
Is royalty a tax?
principles: So a State may tax its land and measure the tax by what the land produces, even where Parliament regulates the industry.

name: Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar
summary: A Bihar surcharge on sales tax, which large dealers could not pass on to buyers, was upheld. A clash under Article 254 arises only between laws on the same Concurrent List subject, and a State tax law is judged by its pith and substance.
question: Bihar levied a surcharge on dealers with sales of more than Rs. 5 lakh a year, and barred them from collecting it from buyers. Was the surcharge valid?
Did the bar on passing on the surcharge clash with the Central price control order?
principles: So the drug makers had to bear the surcharge out of their profits, while patients still paid the controlled price.

name: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd.
summary: The GST Council's recommendations guide Parliament and the State legislatures, but do not bind them. The Court also struck down a separate GST on ocean freight charged to importers who already pay tax on the whole import.
question: Are the recommendations of the GST Council under Article 279A binding on the Union and the States?
Could IGST be charged to an Indian importer, under reverse charge, on the ocean freight for goods imported on CIF terms?
principles: So GST did not make the States give up their power to tax. Each legislature keeps the final say over its own GST law.

name: Atiabari Tea Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam
summary: A tax that directly and immediately holds up the movement of goods restricts the freedom of trade under Article 301. Assam's tax on goods carried by road and inland waterway was struck down, because the procedure in Article 304(b) had not been followed.
question: Can a tax restrict the freedom of trade, commerce and movement under Article 301?
Was the Assam Taxation (on Goods Carried by Roads or Inland Waterways) Act, 1954 valid without the President's permission under Article 304(b)?
principles: So in 1960 the Court treated a tax on moving goods as a barrier to trade. Later benches narrowed this view, and in 2016 nine judges set it aside.

name: K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka
summary: Under Article 300A, a person can be deprived of property only for a public purpose, and the right to compensation is built into the Article. Courts can review a law that takes property. The Karnataka law taking over the Roerich estate was upheld.
question: Does Article 300A require that a law taking a person's property be for a public purpose and provide compensation?
Was the Karnataka law taking over the Roerich estate valid?
principles: So property is no longer a fundamental right, but it is not unprotected. The State must show a public need and pay for what it takes.

name: Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan
summary: Regulatory measures, and compensatory taxes charged for the use of facilities such as roads, do not restrict the freedom of trade under Article 301. Rajasthan's tax on motor vehicles was upheld as a compensatory tax.
question: Is a tax on motor vehicles using a State's roads a restriction on the freedom of trade under Article 301?
Must such a tax meet the conditions of Article 304(b), including the President's prior permission?
principles: So a State could charge buses for using its roads without the President's permission, as long as the charge paid for the roads.

name: Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana
summary: A tax that does not discriminate does not restrict the freedom of trade under Article 301, so States can levy entry tax on goods from other States. The compensatory tax theory was rejected, and earlier judgments were overruled to that extent.
question: Can a tax restrict the freedom of trade, commerce and movement under Article 301?
Is the compensatory tax theory sound?
When does a State tax discriminate against goods from other States under Article 304(a)?
principles: So the question about a State tax is now simple. Does it treat goods from outside worse than local goods? If not, it is valid.

name: In re Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal
summary: Karnataka passed an ordinance to override the Cauvery Tribunal's interim order, and the Court held the ordinance beyond the State's power and unconstitutional. The Tribunal can grant interim relief, and its interim order becomes binding once the Central Government publishes it.
question: Was the Karnataka Cauvery Basin Irrigation Protection Ordinance, 1991 constitutional?
Was the Tribunal's interim order a "report and decision" under Section 5(2) of the 1956 Act, which must be published under Section 6?
Can a Water Disputes Tribunal grant interim relief?
principles: So an upstream State cannot use its position on the river, or its own legislature, to keep the water from a downstream State.

name: Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar Shah
aka: The seven sub-rights of property case
summary: A power to take property and a promise of compensation are not enough. The "authority of law" in Article 300A also requires a fair procedure, which the Court set out as seven rights. The Kolkata Municipal Corporation's claim to have taken a property was invalid.
question: Does Section 352 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980 give the Corporation a power of compulsory acquisition?
What procedure does Article 300A require before a person loses property?
principles: So the State cannot simply write its own name into the property records. The State must follow every step, from notice to a final decision.

name: S.P. Sampath Kumar v. Union of India
summary: The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 was upheld. Judicial review is a basic feature, but in 1986 the Court held that Parliament could replace the High Courts in service disputes with a tribunal that worked equally well. The Court ordered changes to make the tribunal so.
question: Could the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 shut out the High Courts from service matters?
What must a tribunal be like to take the place of a High Court?
principles: So the Court accepted the tribunal, but only after reshaping it to look like a court. Eleven years later, a larger bench went further.

name: All India Judges' Association v. Union of India
summary: Looking again at its 1991 directions, the Court held that judges hold public office and are not employees. The minimum service conditions of the judiciary must be provided whatever a State's finances. The Court changed some directions, including the retirement age of 60.
question: Should the Court change its directions of 13 November 1991 on the service conditions of the subordinate judiciary?
Can States refuse minimum service conditions for judges because they lack money?
principles: So the lower courts cannot be starved of pay, housing and books for want of money. A poor State still owes its judges the basics.

name: Madras Bar Association v. Union of India
summary: The Court struck down the parts of the Tribunals Reforms Ordinance, 2021 that set a minimum age of 50 and a four-year term for tribunal members. The ordinance repeated rules the Court had already rejected, and weakened the independence of tribunals.
question: After the Court's 2020 ruling, could the Ordinance fix a minimum age of 50 for appointment and a four-year term for tribunal members?
Can a law override the Court's directions without removing the basis of its judgment?
principles: So the government cannot keep tribunal members on short terms, always hoping for reappointment. Short terms make them depend on the government they must sometimes rule against.

name: Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner
summary: Article 324 is a store of power for the Election Commission where the law is silent, but the Commission must act fairly and within the law. A challenge to the cancellation of a poll must be made by an election petition after the result, not by a writ petition during the election.
question: Could the High Court hear a writ petition against the Election Commission's order cancelling a poll and ordering a fresh one?
How far does the Election Commission's power under Article 324 reach, and must it follow natural justice?
principles: So the Commission may act quickly to save an election, but it must still act fairly, and it must stand by the reasons it gave at the time.

name: Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms
summary: Voters have a right under Article 19(1)(a) to know about the candidates. The Election Commission was told to require every candidate to declare on affidavit any criminal record, assets, debts and educational qualifications.
question: Do voters have a right to know the criminal record, assets and qualifications of candidates?
Can the Election Commission require such disclosure when the law is silent?
principles: So a voter can now see, before voting, whether a candidate faces serious criminal charges and what the candidate owns.

name: Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India
summary: The Court held that, until Parliament made a law, a committee would advise on appointing the Chief Election Commissioner and the Election Commissioners. The committee was the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice of India. Parliament soon passed a law with a different committee.
question: Was appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner and the Election Commissioners by the government alone consistent with free and fair elections?
Can the Court lay down a procedure for appointment when Parliament has not made the law that Article 324(2) expects?
principles: So the Court tried to take the choice of election referees out of the ruling party's hands alone. Parliament then wrote its own law and kept the government in the majority on the committee.

name: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India
summary: The Electoral Bond Scheme, 2018 was struck down. Secret political funding breaks voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a), and unlimited company donations break Article 14. The State Bank of India was ordered to disclose the details of the bonds.
question: Does secret funding of political parties through electoral bonds break voters' right to information?
Were the amendments allowing unlimited company donations valid?
principles: So voters are entitled to know who pays the parties they vote for, especially when the payer is a company that may want something back.

name: N.P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer, Namakkal Constituency
summary: "Election" in Article 329(b) means the whole process, from the notice of election to the declaration of the result. Once the process begins, courts cannot interfere. The only remedy is an election petition after the election.
question: Can the rejection of a nomination paper be challenged by a writ petition while the election is going on?
What does "election" mean in Article 329(b)?
principles: So a wrongly rejected candidate is not left without a remedy. The remedy simply comes after the vote, so that the election is not held up.

name: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
aka: The private and minority education case
summary: All citizens have a right to set up and run educational institutions, and minorities have a special right under Article 30. Who is a minority is decided State by State. The Unni Krishnan scheme on admissions and fees was struck down, but capitation fees and profiteering are still barred.
question: Who is a minority under Article 30, and is that judged by the State or by the whole country?
Do citizens and minorities have a right to set up and run educational institutions, including professional colleges?
How far can the State control admissions, fees and staff in private and minority institutions, aided and unaided?
Was the Unni Krishnan scheme valid, and was the St. Stephen's College case rightly decided?
principles: So private colleges won control over their own admissions and fees, but lost any right to sell seats.

name: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
summary: Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule on or after 24 April 1973 do not get blanket protection. They can be struck down if they destroy or damage the basic structure, including the rights in Articles 14, 19 and 21.
question: After Kesavananda Bharati, can laws placed in the Ninth Schedule be tested against the basic structure?
How is such a law to be tested?
principles: So the Ninth Schedule is no longer a safe for any law Parliament chooses. A law put there after 1973 must still respect the core of equality, freedom and life.

name: In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution
result: Unanimous in result, in three opinions
summary: The Court upheld the President's orders of August 2019 that ended the special status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370. Article 370 was temporary, and Jammu and Kashmir kept no sovereignty of its own. The Court ordered elections by 30 September 2024, and noted the Union's promise to restore statehood.
question: Did Jammu and Kashmir keep any sovereignty after joining India?
Was Article 370 temporary or permanent?
Could the President end Article 370 after the State's Constituent Assembly had been dissolved, and while the State was under President's Rule?
Was the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 valid?
principles: So the end of the special status stood, even though the Court rejected one of the routes the government had used to reach it.

name: In re: The Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves
summary: Giving Indian territory to another country needs an amendment to the Constitution under Article 368. A law under Article 3 is not enough. The Court also said that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution, a view later rejected in Kesavananda Bharati.
question: Was a law needed to carry out the India-Pakistan agreement on Berubari Union and the Cooch-Behar enclaves?
If so, was a law under Article 3 enough, or was an amendment to the Constitution under Article 368 needed?
principles: So the government cannot hand land to another country by a treaty and an ordinary law. The special majority needed to amend the Constitution must agree.

name: Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister, Maharashtra
result: Unanimous on the State law, 3:2 on the 102nd Amendment
summary: Maharashtra's law giving reservation to the Maratha community was struck down, because it crossed the 50 per cent ceiling without any extraordinary situation. By 3 votes to 2, the Court also held that after the 102nd Amendment, only the President could identify socially and educationally backward classes.
question: Should the 50 per cent ceiling on reservation set in Indra Sawhney be looked at again?
Was the Maharashtra law giving reservation to the Maratha community valid?
After the 102nd Amendment, can States still identify socially and educationally backward classes?
principles: So a large and influential community cannot be added on top of existing quotas just because it asks. The State must prove real backwardness and real necessity.

name: B.K. Pavitra v. Union of India
aka: B.K. Pavitra II, the consequential seniority case
summary: Karnataka's 2018 law giving consequential seniority to Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe employees promoted through reservation was upheld. The State had collected the data that the Court found missing in 2017, so the new law validly cured the defect.
question: Could Karnataka bring back consequential seniority after the Court struck down its 2002 law in B.K. Pavitra I (2017)?
Did the State have enough data on inadequate representation and on administrative efficiency?
principles: So the same rule that failed in 2017 passed in 2019, because this time the State brought the evidence the Court had asked for.

name: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu
summary: The anti-defection law in the Tenth Schedule was upheld, except paragraph 7, which barred courts from hearing disqualification disputes. The Speaker deciding a disqualification acts as a tribunal, and courts can review the decision on limited grounds.
question: Is the Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment (1985), valid?
Was paragraph 7, which barred all courts, valid without ratification by the States?
Can the courts review the Speaker's decision on disqualification?
principles: So the law against defection survived, but the Speaker did not become the final and unchecked judge of it.

name: Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur Legislative Assembly
summary: A Speaker must decide disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule within a reasonable time, normally three months. The Court also urged Parliament to think about giving these decisions to an independent tribunal.
question: Can the courts act when a Speaker does not decide disqualification petitions for a long time?
Within what time should such petitions be decided?
principles: So a Speaker cannot protect a defector simply by sitting on the petition. Silence is treated as a failure the courts can fix.

name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
summary: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including the fundamental rights. But it cannot destroy the basic structure, the core features that make the Constitution what it is. Thirteen judges decided this by 7 votes to 6.
question: Article 368 gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution. Does that power have any limit?
Can Parliament use the power to take away or cut down the fundamental rights in Part III? Six years earlier, in Golak Nath, the Court had said no. Was Golak Nath right?
After Golak Nath, Parliament passed the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments to win back its power and to protect land reform. Were these amendments valid?
principles: Think of a house. Parliament may repair it or add rooms, but may not pull it down and still call it the same house.
The courts decide what belongs to the basic structure, one case at a time. No complete list exists.
So both sides won something. Parliament got back the power that Golak Nath had taken away. The courts kept the last word on whether an amendment goes too far.

name: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
result: Election appeal allowed, clause (4) of Article 329A struck down
summary: The Court did two things. First, the Court struck down clause (4) of Article 329A, which the 39th Amendment had added to declare the Prime Minister's election valid and cancel the High Court's judgment. Free and fair elections are part of the basic structure. Then it decided the election appeal itself, and allowed it under the amended election laws, which it found valid.
question: Could Parliament, by amending the Constitution, declare a disputed election valid and cancel a court's judgment on it?
Can ordinary laws be tested against the basic structure?
Was Indira Gandhi's election to the Lok Sabha in 1971 valid?
principles: So Indira Gandhi kept her seat, but only because Parliament had changed the election law. The Court refused to let Parliament simply declare her the winner.

name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India
aka: The First Judges Case, or the Judges' Transfer case
result: Petitions dismissed, with different majorities on different questions
summary: In appointing judges, consulting the Chief Justice of India does not mean getting his agreement, and the Central Government has the final say. The Court also opened its doors wider, so that lawyers could bring cases about the independence of the judiciary. And it ordered the government's letters on the appointments to be disclosed.
question: Does consultation with the Chief Justice of India in appointing judges mean his agreement, and whose opinion prevails?
Could the government refuse a further term to an additional judge, and transfer a Chief Justice without his consent?
Was the Law Minister's letter of 18 March 1981 valid?
Could practising lawyers bring these cases, and could the government keep its letters on appointments secret?
principles: So in 1981 the government won the power to choose judges. But the case also opened the courts to public interest litigation and to open government.

name: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel
summary: When a case falls under the second proviso to Article 311(2), a civil servant can be dismissed, removed or reduced in rank without any inquiry, and without a hearing even on the penalty. Article 14 and natural justice cannot bring back a hearing that the Constitution itself excludes. Challappan (1975) was overruled.
question: When the second proviso to Article 311(2) applies, is the civil servant entitled to any hearing at all?
Can Article 14 or natural justice require a hearing that the proviso excludes?
When is it "not reasonably practicable" to hold an inquiry under clause (b) of the proviso?
principles: So the government can dismiss without inquiry in these three narrow cases. But it must still record its reasons, and the penalty must still fit the facts.

name: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
summary: The dissolution of the Bihar Legislative Assembly on 23 May 2005 was unconstitutional. The Governor's report rested on no checked facts, and drastic action under Article 356 cannot rest on suspicion. The Court did not restore the Assembly, because fresh elections were already under way.
question: Can a Legislative Assembly be dissolved before its first meeting?
Can an Assembly be dissolved under Article 356 to stop a party from claiming a majority said to be won by illegal means?
Does the Governor's immunity under Article 361 stop the courts from examining the Governor's actions?
If the dissolution is invalid, must the Assembly be restored?
principles: So the Court found that the Assembly had been dissolved without good reason, but did not stop the new elections that had already begun.

name: Prem Nath Kaul v. State of Jammu and Kashmir
summary: Yuvaraj Karan Singh made the Jammu and Kashmir Big Landed Estates Abolition Act in 1950, and the Court held the Act valid. The Yuvaraj held all the Maharaja's powers to make laws. Article 370 did not reduce those powers, because it left the State's final relationship with India to the State's Constituent Assembly.
question: Did Yuvaraj Karan Singh have the power to make the Big Landed Estates Abolition Act in 1950?
Did the Instrument of Accession, Article 370, or the application of parts of the Constitution of India to the State take that power away?
principles: So in 1950 the ruler of Jammu and Kashmir still made its laws, and his land reform, taking land from big landlords without compensation, stood.

name: Rajendra Singh Rana v. Swami Prasad Maurya
summary: Thirteen BSP members of the Uttar Pradesh Assembly asked the Governor to invite the Samajwadi Party to form the government. The Court held that they had voluntarily given up membership of their party, and disqualified them from 27 August 2003. A defence of split needed proof of a split in the party itself, not just a count of legislators.
question: Did the 13 BSP members defect when they asked the Governor to invite the leader of another party to form the government?
Was a split under paragraph 3 shown merely because one-third of the party's legislators broke away?
Could the Supreme Court decide the question of disqualification itself, instead of sending it back to the Speaker?
principles: So the defectors could not escape by adding up legislators. Leaving the party to help a rival form the government was defection.

name: Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra
summary: The Governor of Maharashtra was wrong to call Uddhav Thackeray to a floor test in June 2022. But the Thackeray government could not be restored, because Thackeray resigned without facing the vote. The political party, not its legislators, appoints the whip. Whether Nabam Rebia was right was sent to seven judges.
question: Can a Speaker facing a notice for removal decide disqualification petitions, which Nabam Rebia had said a Speaker cannot do?
Who appoints the whip and the party's leader in the House: the political party or the legislature party?
Was the Governor right to call for a floor test, and to invite Eknath Shinde to form the government?
Can the Speaker and the Election Commission act at the same time on rival claims to be the real party?
principles: So the Court found the Governor at fault, but could not undo a resignation. A Chief Minister who steps down before the vote cannot later be put back.

name: Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi
summary: A society that works as an arm of the government is "the State" under Article 12, so it must respect fundamental rights. Giving one-third of the admission marks to a two-minute interview was arbitrary and broke Article 14.
question: A registered society ran a government-funded engineering college. Is the society "the State" under Article 12?
The college gave one-third of the admission marks to an oral interview. Was that arbitrary, and so a breach of Article 14?
principles: Six signs help show that a body is an arm of the government. The government holds its shares. Government money meets almost all its costs. The State gives or protects its monopoly.
The other three signs are deep and pervasive control by the State, work of public importance close to the work of government, and a government department handed over to the body.
The signs are indicators, not a checklist that must be fully met.
The Court also said that interview marks should not be more than 15 per cent of the total, because an interview is so easy to misuse.
So what matters is whether a body is the government in substance, whatever it calls itself.

name: Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology
summary: The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research is "the State" under Article 12. A body is "the State" if the government dominates it in money, functions and administration.
question: CSIR is a registered society. Is it "the State" under Article 12?
Was Sabhajit Tewary, which said CSIR is not "the State", rightly decided?
principles: The test applies to any kind of body, whether a statute set it up or it was registered as a company or a society.
No single sign settles the question. A body that shows one or two of the Ajay Hasia signs may still fall outside Article 12.
So the test looks at who really runs the body, not at the form on its papers.

name: Zee Telefilms Ltd. v. Union of India
summary: The Board of Control for Cricket in India is not "the State" under Article 12, so it cannot be taken straight to the Supreme Court under Article 32. But because it does public work, it can be taken to a High Court under Article 226.
question: Is the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) "the State" under Article 12, so that a writ petition can be filed against it in the Supreme Court under Article 32?
principles: There are two routes with two tests. Article 32 needs "the State", but Article 226 needs only a public duty.
So a body can stay outside Article 12 and still answer in court for the way it does public work.

name: Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India
summary: The First Amendment was valid. An amendment to the Constitution is not an ordinary "law" under Article 13(2), so Parliament could use it to change the fundamental rights.
question: Is an amendment to the Constitution a "law" under Article 13(2), so that it is void if it takes away or cuts down a fundamental right?
Was the First Amendment (1951) made in the proper way?
principles: The power to amend is a constituent power, different in kind from the power to make ordinary laws.
So in 1951 the text placed no limit on what Parliament could amend, the fundamental rights included.

name: I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab
summary: By 6 votes to 5, Parliament could not amend the Constitution to take away or cut down the fundamental rights. To avoid upsetting the past, the ruling applied only to future amendments.
question: Can Parliament use Article 368 to take away or cut down the fundamental rights in Part III?
Is an amendment to the Constitution a "law" under Article 13(2)?
Were Sankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1964) rightly decided?
principles: Prospective overruling entered Indian law here. A court can lay down a new rule for the future while leaving past decisions undisturbed.
So the Court protected the fundamental rights for the future without undoing the land reforms already made.

name: Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay
summary: Fundamental rights do not reach back into the past. A prosecution for an act done before 26 January 1950 could continue, even though the law behind it clashed with a fundamental right.
question: Does Article 13(1) reach back to acts done before 26 January 1950?
A prosecution began before the Constitution came into force, under a law that clashed with a fundamental right. Could it continue after 26 January 1950?
principles: The Constitution does not undo the past. Completed acts, and prosecutions for them, are judged by the law that applied when the acts were done.
So a clashing law from before 1950 is not wiped off the books. The law only stops working against rights from 26 January 1950, an idea the Court later built into the doctrine of eclipse.

name: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh
summary: A law from before the Constitution that clashed with a fundamental right was not dead, only eclipsed. When the First Amendment removed the clash, the law worked again without being passed afresh.
question: A law made before the Constitution clashed with Article 19(1)(g) from 1950. Did the law die for ever, or could it come back to life when an amendment removed the clash?
principles: The rule is called the doctrine of eclipse. A clash with a fundamental right puts an old law to sleep, but does not kill it.
So when the clash ends, an old law needs no new vote of the legislature to work again.

name: R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India
summary: When only part of a law is invalid, the valid part survives if it can be separated from the rest. The Prize Competitions Act covered only gambling competitions, so it was valid.
question: The Prize Competitions Act, 1955 defined "prize competition" widely. Did the definition cover competitions of skill as well as gambling competitions?
If it did, and the part about competitions of skill was invalid, did the whole Act fail? Or could the valid part be separated and saved?
principles: The main test is what the legislature intended. Would it have passed the valid part alone if it had known that the rest was invalid?
If the valid part is distinct and complete in itself, the valid part survives.
If the valid and invalid parts form one scheme meant to work as a whole, the whole law fails.
If what is left is so thin that it differs from what the legislature passed, or cannot work without rewriting, the whole law fails.
Substance matters more than form. Valid and invalid parts can sit in the same section. The history, purpose, title and preamble of a law help show what the legislature intended.
So a court cuts away only the bad part of a law, as long as what remains is still the law the legislature meant to make.

name: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar
summary: A law let the government send any case it liked to a special court, where the accused got fewer protections. Because nothing guided that choice, the law broke the equal protection promised by Article 14.
question: Section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 let the State Government send "offences", "classes of offences", "cases" or "classes of cases" to a Special Court. Did that power break the equal protection of the laws under Article 14?
principles: A law need not discriminate on its face to break Article 14. A power to discriminate, with nothing to guide it, is enough.
Equal protection reaches procedure as well as substance.
So the problem was not the special court itself, but a power to send anyone there with nothing to guide the choice.

name: Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S.R. Tendolkar
summary: A law may treat a group differently if two tests are met. The line must separate the group by a clear difference, and the difference must be linked to the law's purpose. On that test, an inquiry into the Dalmia companies was upheld.
question: Did the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952, and an order setting up an inquiry into certain companies, break Article 14?
What test decides whether a law may treat a group differently under Article 14?
principles: A law is presumed to be constitutional. The person who challenges it must show that it discriminates.
A law may apply to a single person or company, if special circumstances make that person a class by itself.
A law that picks out one person for special treatment without any reasonable basis is void.
A law that gives the government a choice without any policy to guide it is void. But if the law states a policy and the government ignores it, only the government's action is struck down.
So a law may single out even one company, as long as a real difference sets it apart and the difference serves the law's purpose.

name: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
summary: Equality is the opposite of arbitrariness, so an arbitrary act of the State breaks Articles 14 and 16. On the facts, the transfer of Tamil Nadu's Chief Secretary was upheld.
question: Did moving the Chief Secretary of Tamil Nadu to other posts break Articles 14 and 16?
Was he moved in bad faith?
principles: Article 14 now has two tests. One checks the line a law draws between groups. The other, from this case, checks whether State action is arbitrary.
So Royappa lost his own case, but the reasoning changed Article 14. Any arbitrary act of the State can now be challenged as a denial of equality.

name: Air India v. Nergesh Meerza
summary: Air India's rule that ended an air hostess's job on her first pregnancy was struck down as plainly arbitrary. So was the unguided power of the Managing Director to extend her service.
question: Did the service rules for air hostesses in Air India and Indian Airlines discriminate against women under Articles 14, 15 and 16?
Were the rules on retirement at 35, on marriage and on first pregnancy arbitrary?
principles: Articles 14 and 15 work differently. Article 15 bars only discrimination on the ground of sex alone, but Article 14 strikes at any rule that is plainly arbitrary.
So a rule can survive the ban on sex discrimination and still fall as arbitrary.

name: D.S. Nakara v. Union of India
summary: All pensioners form one class. A better pension formula given only to those who retired after a chosen date was arbitrary, so the Court extended it to all pensioners from that date.
question: The government gave a better pension formula only to those who retired on or after a chosen date in 1979. Did dividing pensioners by their date of retirement break Article 14?
principles: A cut-off date that splits one class must have a rational link to the purpose of the scheme. An arbitrary date breaks Article 14.
Pension is deferred pay earned by long service, and a form of social security in old age.
The Court read pensions together with Article 41 and the idea of a socialist welfare State in the Preamble.
So the government could not give two people with the same service different pensions only because one retired a day later.

name: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
summary: Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code made adultery a crime and treated a wife as her husband's property. The Court struck it down. Adultery is still a ground for divorce.
question: Is Section 497 IPC, which made adultery a crime, valid under Articles 14, 15 and 21?
Is Section 198(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which let only the husband complain, valid?
principles: Manifest arbitrariness is a ground for striking down a law, not only an executive act.
Laws that rest on stereotypes about women fail Article 15, even when they seem to protect women.
Criminal law should not be used to punish private conduct between adults in a marriage.
So the State may still let adultery end a marriage, but it may not send a person to prison for it.

name: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
summary: A Madras order that shared out college seats by religion and caste broke Article 29(2). The Court also held that the Directive Principles cannot override the fundamental rights.
question: The Communal G.O. divided seats in State medical and engineering colleges among religions and castes. Did the order break Article 29(2)?
Could Article 46, the Directive Principle on helping the weaker sections, save the order?
principles: A fundamental right gives way only to an exception written into the Constitution. A policy goal, however worthy, cannot create one.
So the Constitution of 1951 allowed reservation in jobs but not in education, and Parliament closed that gap the same year.

name: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
summary: The amendments that allow reservation in promotion, with the seniority that comes with it, are valid. But a State that uses them must show, with data, backwardness and too little representation, and must keep the administration efficient.
question: The 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments allowed reservation in promotion for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Did they destroy the basic structure?
principles: An amendment is tested by two questions. Does it widen a power so far that the limits on it disappear? Does it destroy the identity of the Constitution?
So Parliament could allow reservation in promotion, but each State had to justify it with evidence before using it.

name: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta
summary: M. Nagaraj did not need a larger bench. But its demand that States prove the backwardness of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes with data was wrong. And the creamy layer rule can apply to them.
question: Should M. Nagaraj (2006) be sent to a bench of seven judges to be looked at again?
Must a State collect data to prove the backwardness of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes before giving them reservation in promotion?
Does the creamy layer rule apply to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
principles: The creamy layer rule comes from equality itself, not from any one scheme. So the rule can reach every group that gets reservation.
So the judgment removed one hurdle for the States and added one limit. Backwardness needs no proof, but the creamy layer can be left out.

name: State of Karnataka v. Appa Balu Ingale
summary: Villagers who stopped Dalits from drawing water from a new borewell, calling them "untouchables", were guilty under the Protection of Civil Rights Act. Article 17 binds private persons, not only the State.
question: Were the accused guilty of enforcing untouchability under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955?
How far do Article 17 and the Act reach the conduct of private persons?
principles: Some fundamental rights bind private persons, because the text says so. Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24 are the clearest examples.
So a villager who keeps a Dalit away from a public well commits a crime, even though no official is involved.

name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
summary: Reserving 27 per cent of central government jobs for backward classes was upheld. But the better-off among them, the creamy layer, must be left out, total reservation should not normally cross 50 per cent, and there can be no reservation in promotions.
question: Was the order reserving 27 per cent of central government posts for socially and educationally backward classes valid under Article 16(4)?
Can caste be used to identify a backward class? Can income or wealth alone be used?
Is there a limit on how much can be reserved? Does reservation reach promotions?
principles: Article 16(4) is not an exception to Article 16(1). Article 16(4) is a way of reaching the equality that Article 16(1) promises.
So the Court accepted reservation for the backward classes, but fenced it in, so that it helps those who need it most and does not swallow equal opportunity.

name: Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India
aka: The OBC reservation in higher education case
summary: The Court upheld the 93rd Amendment and the 27 per cent reservation for Other Backward Classes in central colleges and universities, for those run or aided by the State. The creamy layer must be left out.
question: Is the 93rd Amendment (2005), which added Article 15(5), valid?
Is the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006, which reserved 27 per cent of seats for Other Backward Classes, valid?
Must the creamy layer be left out of this reservation?
principles: Article 15(5) only enables the State to make special measures in education for backward classes. The clause does not force it to.
So the creamy layer rule, first set for jobs in Indra Sawhney, now limits reservation in education too.

name: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India
summary: By 3 votes to 2, the Court upheld the 103rd Amendment. Reserving up to 10 per cent for economically weaker sections, while leaving out classes that already have reservation, does not break the basic structure.
question: Does the 103rd Amendment break the basic structure by allowing reservation on economic grounds alone?
Does it break the basic structure by allowing such reservation in private colleges that take no government money?
Does it break the basic structure by leaving out the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes from this reservation?
principles: Equality lets the State give different groups different kinds of help. Leaving a group out of one scheme is fair when it already has its own.
So reservation in India now has two bases. Social and educational backwardness remains one, and poverty among those without other reservation is the second.

name: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
summary: The Court struck down a ban on a journal entering Madras. Freedom of speech includes the freedom to circulate what one publishes, and in 1950 "public safety" was not a ground for limiting speech.
question: Does freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) include the freedom to circulate a journal?
A law allowed limits on speech for "public safety" or "the maintenance of public order". Could that law be saved by Article 19(2) as it stood in 1950?
principles: Freedom of the press is not named in Article 19, but it is part of freedom of speech.
The grounds for limiting speech are a closed list. A ground that is not in Article 19(2) cannot be used, however sensible it seems.
So in 1950 the government could not ban a journal merely to keep public order. Parliament changed the Constitution the next year to allow it.

name: Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India
summary: The Court struck down a law that fixed how many pages a newspaper could print for its price. The State cannot cut down speech in order to regulate the business side of a newspaper.
question: Did the Newspaper (Price and Page) Act, 1956 and the Daily Newspaper (Price and Page) Order, 1960 break freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a)?
principles: Each freedom carries its own list of limits. The grounds in Article 19(6) for regulating trade cannot be used to limit speech.
So a newspaper is first a voice and only then a business. A law that shrinks the voice must pass the test for speech.

name: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India
summary: The newsprint policy of 1972-73 capped newspapers at ten pages and stopped big groups from starting new editions. The Court held that it broke freedom of the press. What matters is the direct effect of a measure on the right, not its stated aim.
question: Could newspaper companies and their shareholders challenge the newsprint policy under Article 32?
Did the newsprint import policy for 1972-73 break Articles 19(1)(a) and 14?
principles: Shareholders can claim their own Article 19 rights when a law hits the company they own.
So the government cannot escape the test for speech by calling a measure an economic policy. The Court looks at what the measure does.

name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
summary: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act punished online messages that were "grossly offensive" or caused "annoyance". The Court struck it down because those words are vague and catch far too much speech.
question: Is Section 66A of the Information Technology Act valid under Article 19(1)(a), or is it saved by Article 19(2)?
Are the rules for blocking websites under Section 69A, and the duties of intermediaries under Section 79, valid?
principles: A vague law on speech harms even people who are never charged, because they stay silent to be safe. Courts call this the chilling effect.
So people may argue for any cause online, however unpopular. The law can step in only when speech incites harm.

name: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
summary: Speech and business over the internet are protected by Article 19. An internet shutdown cannot last indefinitely, and every order must be published, proportionate and reviewed.
question: Can the government refuse to produce the orders that imposed the restrictions?
Is freedom of speech and of business over the internet protected by Article 19?
Were the internet shutdown and the orders under Section 144 in Jammu and Kashmir valid?
principles: Any limit on a fundamental right must be proportionate. The State must choose the least restrictive measure that will work.
So the government may cut the internet in an emergency, but only for a limited time, on the record, and under regular review.

name: State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad
summary: Making an accused give samples of handwriting, signatures or fingerprints does not force him to be a witness against himself, so Article 20(3) is not broken.
question: Does taking sample handwriting or fingerprints from an accused force him "to be a witness against himself" under Article 20(3)?
Does being in police custody, by itself, amount to force?
principles: So the line runs between the mind and the body. The police may take a person's fingerprints, but may not force out what the person knows.

name: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
summary: No one can be forced to undergo narcoanalysis, a lie detector test or brain mapping. Forcing these tests breaks the right against self-incrimination and the right to personal liberty.
question: Can a person be made to undergo narcoanalysis, a polygraph test or a Brain Electrical Activation Profile (BEAP) test without consent?
Do these tests break Article 20(3) and Article 21?
principles: Mental privacy is part of personal liberty under Article 21.
So the State may take a suspect's fingerprints, but it may not reach into the suspect's mind without consent.

name: Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay
summary: When customs officers confiscated smuggled gold, that was not "prosecution and punishment" by a court. So a later criminal trial for the same act did not break Article 20(2).
question: A traveller's gold was confiscated by the customs authorities. Did Article 20(2) then stop his later prosecution under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act?
principles: Article 20(2) is narrower than the rule against double jeopardy in some other countries. A second trial is barred only after a first prosecution has ended in punishment.
So a person can lose smuggled goods to the customs and still face a criminal trial for the smuggling.

name: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala
summary: Three schoolchildren stood respectfully during the national anthem but did not sing it, because of their faith. The Court held that they could not be expelled, since no law makes anyone sing it.
question: Could students be expelled for standing respectfully during the national anthem but not singing it, because their religion forbade it?
Did the expulsion break Articles 19(1)(a) and 25?
principles: A right can be limited only by a law. An official's circular, however well meant, is not enough.

The judgment closes on tolerance. Justice Chinnappa Reddy wrote that India's tradition teaches tolerance, its philosophy preaches tolerance and its Constitution practises tolerance, and he asked: "let us not dilute it."
So respect for the anthem can be shown by standing in silence. The State cannot force children to sing against their faith.

name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
summary: Any procedure set out in a valid law was enough to satisfy Article 21, whether or not it was fair. The Preventive Detention Act, 1950 was upheld, except the section that hid the reasons for detention from the courts.
question: Does "procedure established by law" in Article 21 mean any procedure laid down by a law, or a fair procedure?
Must a law of preventive detention also pass the tests in Article 19, which protects freedoms such as free movement?
Was the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 valid?
principles: The case stood for reading each fundamental right on its own, as if each covered a separate field. Later cases rejected that idea.
So the State could detain a person by following any procedure that a law set out. Twenty-eight years later, Maneka Gandhi turned this round.

name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
summary: A procedure that takes away personal liberty must be right, just and fair, not arbitrary. Articles 14, 19 and 21 must be read together, and the right to go abroad is part of personal liberty.
question: Is the right to travel abroad part of "personal liberty" under Article 21?
Is any procedure laid down by law enough under Article 21, or must the procedure be fair?
Must a law that takes away personal liberty also pass the tests in Articles 14 and 19?
Could a passport be taken away without giving the holder a hearing or reasons?
principles: Articles 14, 19 and 21 together are often called the "golden triangle".
Natural justice, such as the right to be heard, can be read into a law that says nothing about it.
So after 1978 the question is not only whether a law allows the State to take away liberty. The question is also whether the law and its procedure are fair.

name: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
summary: A speedy trial is part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21. The State must give free legal aid to those who cannot pay, and it cannot plead lack of money to deny a speedy trial.
question: Does Article 21 give an accused person the right to a speedy trial?
What must the State do for undertrial prisoners who have been in jail for years without trial?
principles: A shortage of money is no defence when a fundamental right is at stake. The State must find the means to protect the right.
So a poor person cannot be left in jail for years simply because the system is slow. The delay itself breaks Article 21.

name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
summary: The right to life includes the right to livelihood. The city could remove pavement dwellers under the law, but only by a fair procedure, and the Court gave directions for their resettlement.
question: Can a person give up a fundamental right and lose the power to claim it later?
Does the right to life under Article 21 include the right to livelihood?
Is Section 314 of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, which allows encroachments to be removed without notice, valid?
principles: Even a lawful power to evict must be used by a fair procedure.
So the pavement dwellers had no right to stay on the pavement for ever. But the State could not throw them out without notice, a hearing and a thought for where they would go.

name: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
summary: Sexual harassment at work breaks Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21. Because no law dealt with it, the Court laid down binding guidelines, drawing on international conventions.
question: Does sexual harassment of women at work break their fundamental rights?
With no law in place, can the Court lay down binding rules, using international conventions that India has ratified?
principles: When the legislature is silent on a fundamental right, the Court can lay down binding guidelines under Article 32 that last until Parliament acts.
So the Court did not wait for Parliament. The Court wrote rules that bound every workplace until Parliament acted, sixteen years later.

name: Common Cause v. Union of India
summary: The right to die with dignity is part of Article 21. Passive euthanasia and living wills are lawful, with safeguards. Active euthanasia is not allowed.
question: Does the right to live with dignity under Article 21 include the right to die with dignity?
Is passive euthanasia lawful? Are living wills valid?
