principles: The right to refuse treatment comes from a person's autonomy over their own body. Doctors must respect it even when the refusal will lead to death.
So a person may choose not to be kept alive by machines. But no one may act to end another person's life.

name: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
summary: Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code was struck down so far as it made consensual sex between adults a crime. Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013) was overruled.
question: Is Section 377 valid, so far as it makes consensual sex between adults of the same sex a crime?
Was Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013), which upheld Section 377, rightly decided?
principles: Discrimination because of sexual orientation is discrimination because of sex under Article 15.
So a right protects a minority even when most people disapprove. The Constitution's values decide, not a vote.

name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
summary: Torture in police custody breaks Article 21, and the State must pay compensation for it. The Court laid down requirements that the police must follow at every arrest and detention.
question: What safeguards must the police follow when they arrest and hold a person, to prevent violence in custody?
Must the State pay compensation for deaths and torture in custody?
principles: Compensation for breaking a fundamental right comes in addition to the ordinary remedies. A victim may still sue for damages in the ordinary courts.
So every arrest must leave a record: who arrested whom, when, where, and in what condition. Torture becomes harder to hide.

name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India
summary: A business that carries on a hazardous activity is absolutely liable for any harm it causes, with no exceptions. The compensation must match the size and wealth of the business.
question: Can the Supreme Court award compensation under Article 32 for the breach of fundamental rights?
How far is a business in a hazardous industry liable when an accident harms people?
Is a private company such as Shriram "the State" under Article 12?
principles: Indian courts may make new rules of liability to suit Indian conditions, instead of following English law.
So a dangerous industry pays for every accident it causes. Unlike strict liability, absolute liability allows no excuse such as an act of God.

name: A.K. Roy v. Union of India
result: Act upheld, two judges partly dissenting
summary: The National Security Act, 1980, a preventive detention law, was upheld. The Court laid down safeguards for people held under it. But it held that it could not order the government to bring the 44th Amendment's changes to Article 22 into force.
question: Is an ordinance a "law" under Article 21, so that it can take away personal liberty?
Can the Court order the Central Government to bring Section 3 of the 44th Amendment into force?
Are the grounds of detention in the National Security Act too vague?
What rights does a detenu have before the Advisory Board and during detention?
principles: A ground of detention must give fair warning. People must be able to know in advance what conduct can get them detained.
So the Court made detention more humane, but it could not force the government to bring in the stronger safeguard that Parliament had already passed.

name: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India
summary: Paying a worker less than the minimum wage is forced labour under Article 23. Articles 23 and 24 bind private employers too, and a government that hires contractors must make sure they obey the labour laws.
question: Can an organisation bring a case for workers who cannot come to court themselves?
Does paying less than the minimum wage amount to "forced labour" under Article 23?
Do Articles 23 and 24 apply against private contractors?
Are the government bodies that hired the contractors responsible when the contractors break the labour laws?
principles: Article 23 reaches beyond slavery and begar, to any work drawn out of a person by economic pressure.
So a worker who accepts a low wage because of hunger has not chosen freely. Paying less than the minimum is forcing the worker.

name: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
summary: The right to live with human dignity under Article 21 protects workers from exploitation. Where a labourer is made to do forced labour, the Court presumes that the labourer is bonded, and the State must enforce the welfare laws.
question: Can a letter to the Court about bonded labourers be treated as a writ petition under Article 32?
Can the Court appoint commissioners to find the facts?
What must the State do for labourers held in bondage in stone quarries?
principles: Directive Principles can give content to a fundamental right. The welfare goals in Part IV shape what dignity under Article 21 requires.
So the burden shifted. A quarry owner who keeps workers in forced labour must prove that they are not bonded, instead of the workers proving that they are.

name: Rev. Stainislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh
summary: The right to propagate religion under Article 25 does not include a right to convert another person. State laws that punish conversion by force, fraud or allurement are valid.
question: Does the right to "propagate" religion under Article 25(1) include the right to convert others?
Could the States of Madhya Pradesh and Orissa make laws against forcible conversion, or was the subject for Parliament alone?
principles: So a person may preach and explain a faith freely. But the State may punish conversions brought about by pressure, trickery or bribes.

name: Durgah Committee, Ajmer v. Syed Hussain Ali
summary: Article 26 protects only the rights that a religious denomination already had, and creates no new ones. The Durgah Khawaja Saheb Act, 1955 was upheld, and the Court warned that practices born of superstition may not be protected.
question: Did the Durgah Khawaja Saheb Act, 1955 break the rights of the Khadims and of the Chishtia Sufis under Articles 25 and 26?
Did it break the Khadims' right to property under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31?
principles: The essential practices test lets courts separate the core of a faith from later additions, and protect only the core.
So a denomination cannot use Article 26 to win control it never had.

name: M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu
summary: Children in hazardous jobs must be taken out of work and sent to school. The employer must pay Rs. 20,000 for each child into a welfare fund, and the government must find a job for an adult in the family or pay in Rs. 5,000.
question: How should the ban in Article 24 on employing children in hazardous work be enforced?
What should happen to children taken out of such work, and to their families?
principles: The ban on child labour in hazardous work must be backed by rehabilitation and education, not only by punishment.
Articles 39(e), 39(f), 41, 45 and 47 guide how Article 24 is enforced.
So the Court tackled the reason children work, which is family poverty. The family gets a job or an income only while the child stays in school.

name: Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt
summary: What is essential to a religion is decided by that religion's own doctrines. A religious denomination can manage its own affairs in matters of religion, and the State can regulate only the secular side. Several sections of the Madras Act were struck down.
question: What does "religion" mean in Articles 25 and 26, and what is a "religious denomination"?
How far can the State control the running of a Math and its property?
Did the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 break Articles 19(1)(f), 25 and 26?
Was the yearly contribution charged under Section 76 of the Act a fee or a tax?
principles: The State's power over a religious institution runs through its property and administration, not through its rituals.
So the State may check a Math's accounts, but it cannot take over its religious life or run it through its own manager.

name: Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala
summary: By 4 votes to 1, the Court struck down the bar on women aged 10 to 50 entering the Sabarimala temple. The devotees of Lord Ayyappa are not a separate denomination, and the exclusion is not an essential religious practice. Wider questions from the case are now before nine judges.
question: Does keeping out women aged 10 to 50 break Articles 14, 15, 17 and 25?
Is the exclusion an essential religious practice protected by Articles 25 and 26?
Are the devotees of Lord Ayyappa a separate religious denomination?
Is Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965 valid?
principles: A believer's right to worship in a public temple can prevail over a custom that is not essential to the faith.
So in 2018 equality won over custom. But the dissent, and the review that followed, show that the balance between faith and equality is still being argued.

name: Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra
summary: A final judgment of the Supreme Court cannot be challenged by a writ petition under Article 32. But the Court can look again at its own final judgment through a "curative petition", in rare cases, to stop abuse of its process and to cure a gross injustice.
question: After a review petition has been dismissed, can a final judgment of the Supreme Court be challenged by a writ petition under Article 32?
Is a person wronged by such a judgment left with any remedy at all?
principles: The Court's inherent power to do justice can create a remedy that no statute or rule provides.
So finality and justice are balanced. The door to reopen a final judgment exists, but it is narrow and heavily guarded.

name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
summary: Parliament cannot use its limited power to amend the Constitution to make that power unlimited. The Court struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368, and the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all the Directive Principles.
question: Were clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368, added by the 42nd Amendment, valid?
Was the 42nd Amendment's change to Article 31C valid? The change protected laws carrying out any Directive Principle from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
principles: So the Emergency's attempt to put amendments beyond the courts failed. The limit set in Kesavananda Bharati protects itself.

name: Waman Rao v. Union of India
summary: Amendments made before 24 April 1973, the date of Kesavananda Bharati, cannot be challenged for damaging the basic structure. Amendments made on or after that date can be, including those that added laws to the Ninth Schedule.
question: Are Article 31A and the original Article 31C valid under the basic structure doctrine?
Can laws placed in the Ninth Schedule be challenged, and does the date of the amendment that placed them there matter?
Were the Maharashtra land ceiling laws valid?
principles: A fixed date can separate what is settled from what stays open to challenge. The Court chose the day the basic structure test began.
So the land reforms of the 1950s and 1960s were made safe for good, while everything Parliament did after 1973 stays open to the basic structure test.

name: Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra
summary: Not every privately owned resource is a "material resource of the community" under Article 39(b). Whether it is depends on its nature, scarcity and other factors. All nine judges held that Article 31C, in the form upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, is still in force.
question: Is Article 31C still in force after Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment's change to it?
Do the "material resources of the community" in Article 39(b) include all privately owned resources?
principles: So the State can still use Article 31C to protect laws that share out resources. But it cannot treat every private flat or factory as community property just by saying so.

name: Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India
summary: A Hindu husband who converts to Islam cannot marry again while his first marriage lasts. The second marriage is void, and he is guilty of bigamy. The Court urged the government to work towards a uniform civil code.
question: Does a Hindu marriage end when the husband converts to Islam?
Is a second marriage after such a conversion valid, and is the husband guilty of bigamy under Section 494?
principles: So a husband cannot change his religion to change the rules of a marriage he has already made.

name: State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat
summary: Gujarat's total ban on slaughtering cows and their progeny, including bulls and bullocks of any age, was upheld as a reasonable limit. The Court read the Directive Principles in Articles 48 and 48A, and the duty in Article 51A(g), together with the right to trade.
question: Is a total ban on slaughtering bulls and bullocks of any age a reasonable limit on the butchers' right to trade under Article 19(1)(g)?
How far can the Directive Principles and the fundamental duties justify limits on fundamental rights?
principles: Reasonableness is judged by the conditions of the time. When the facts behind an older ruling change, the answer can change too.
So Quareshi's rule of 1958 gave way. A State may now protect all cattle, useful or not, without breaking the right to trade.

name: Society for Un-aided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India
aka: The RTE 25 per cent quota case
summary: The Right to Education Act, 2009 is valid. Its rule that schools must give 25 per cent of seats to children from weaker and disadvantaged groups applies to private schools that take no government money, but not to such schools run by minorities.
question: Is the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 valid?
Can Section 12(1)(c), which reserves 25 per cent of Class I seats for children from weaker sections and disadvantaged groups, apply to unaided private schools?
Does the Act apply to minority schools?
principles: So a poor child can claim a free seat in a private neighbourhood school, with the State paying, unless the school is a minority school.

name: AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS
summary: AIIMS reserved 33 per cent of its postgraduate seats for its own graduates, and the Court struck the reservation down. The Court allowed a smaller preference of 25 per cent, and relied on the citizen's duty to strive towards excellence.
question: Was the reservation of postgraduate seats at AIIMS for its own graduates valid under Article 14?
What part do the fundamental duties in Article 51A play in deciding such questions?
principles: Merit weighs more as education rises. A preference that is fair for entry to college is harder to justify at the postgraduate level.
So a college may favour its own students a little, but not so much that better candidates from elsewhere are shut out.

name: Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal
summary: An institution does not lose minority status under Article 30 just because a law of Parliament incorporated it. Azeez Basha (1967) was overruled, and a regular bench will decide, using the new test, whether AMU is a minority institution.
question: Can an educational institution incorporated by a law be a minority institution under Article 30(1)?
What shows that an institution was "established" by a minority?
Was Azeez Basha rightly decided?
principles: Article 30 looks to the past. The question is who founded an institution, so the evidence lies in its early history.
So AMU's status is not settled yet. The Court changed the test, and a smaller bench must now apply it to AMU's history.
